guideTitle: Best Snow Blowers for Gravel Driveways (2026)
metaTitle: Best Snow Blowers for Gravel Driveways (2026)
metaDescription: Five snow blowers compared for gravel driveways: two-stage gas and battery machines with adjustable skid shoes, plus one single-stage for paved sections.
expertTake: A gravel drive calls for a two-stage machine with adjustable skid shoes, and the Husqvarna ST124 is the best all-round pick. The EGO SNT2425 is the quiet battery alternative and the BILT HARD is the budget gas option. Avoid single-stage machines for the gravel itself, because their auger scrapes the surface and throws stones. Raise the skid shoes before the first pass. Add spare skid shoes to the order.
introParagraphs: Gravel changes the rules for choosing a machine. A single-stage auger rides on the surface and flings loose stone through the chute, which can damage windows, cars and the machine itself, so the design has to lift off the ground. A tidy gravel drive in winter is mostly a matter of setting the machine up correctly.

What matters on gravel is the ability to raise the housing, a drive that holds traction on loose footing and an intake that clears snow without scalping stone. Those features sit on two-stage machines, and the rest of this guide is about which one suits your drive. Read the specs for skid shoes and intake height before you read the price. A short test on a small patch of the drive shows whether the setting is right.

products.name: Husqvarna ST124 24-inch 212cc two-stage
products.description:
The ST124 is a two-stage gas machine, which is the right design for gravel because the auger housing sits above the surface instead of scraping it. A 212cc engine drives a ribbon auger that blends air into the snow, and 13-inch snow tires give grip on loose footing.

The 21-inch intake lets it take a tall pile in one pass, which reduces the number of times you set the housing low. Set the skid shoes so the auger sits about an inch above the stone, leaving a thin layer of snow rather than scalping the drive.

Ownership is the usual gas routine of fresh fuel, oil and shear pin checks. On gravel, inspect the scraper bar and skid shoes more often because stone wears them quickly. Plan on carrying spare shear pins and a skid shoe set, since gravel is the hardest surface a snow machine meets. If your lane is steep, consider chains for the tires before the first storm. It is also a machine you can lift by the handle to pivot when the surface is loose.
products.bestFor: Gravel drives where traction and a raised housing both matter.
pros: Two-stage design keeps the auger above the stone
cons: Heavy and noisy compared with electric
Skid shoes wear faster on stone

products.name: EGO Power+ SNT2425 24-inch two-stage, 2 x 7.5Ah

specList.label: Rated coverage
specList.value: Up to 18 cars in 8 in snow

products.description:
The SNT2425 is the one battery-powered two-stage that makes sense on a gravel drive. A separate auger and impeller mean the housing can sit above the stone, and the maker claims up to a 50-foot throw.

Against the gas models it is quieter and starts at the push of a button, but gravel is hard on battery machines because loose footing and tall piles draw more current. Plan on fewer cars per charge than the listing's 18-car rating, which is for 8 inches of light snow on pavement.

Store the packs indoors, charge them before the forecast and check the skid shoes each season. A cold battery on a gravel lane can feel weaker, so bring the packs in after each session and start with a full pair. If your lane is longer than about 150 feet, a second pair of packs is worth the cost. If you pair it with a charger that stays indoors, startup is the easiest of the group.
products.bestFor: Gravel drives where fuel-free operation matters and snow is moderate.
cons: Runtime shrinks on gravel and in wet snow

products.name: PowerSmart 26-inch 252cc two-stage, 120V electric start
products.description:
This is a larger gas two-stage with a 252cc engine, an all-steel auger and a high-speed steel impeller. The listing says it throws up to 45 feet and moves 2,650 pounds per minute.

The all-steel auger is a plus on gravel because it handles the occasional stone better than a plastic or rubber part. A bigger engine gives headroom on a long gravel lane where you plow slowly.

It is a value-priced option, so check parts availability. Use fresh fuel and watch the skid shoes. On a long lane, fuel use matters, so keep a fresh can near the garage and refill the tank only when the engine is cool. Treat the large engine as headroom for slow passes on loose footing. A big engine also means more fuel and a louder start, so plan accordingly.
products.bestFor: Long gravel lanes needing a big engine and a steel auger.
pros: 252cc engine with 2,650 lb per minute rating

products.name: BILT HARD 24-inch 212cc two-stage, serrated augers
products.description:
The BILT HARD is a 24-inch two-stage with 10-inch serrated steel augers and a self-propelled drive with six forward and two reverse speeds. Electric start and LED lighting are fitted.

Serrated steel augers bite into compacted snow and ice, which helps on a gravel drive where snow packs under traffic. As a two-stage it can sit above the stone with the skid shoes raised.

As with any value brand, check parts and warranty before you buy. Check parts availability for skid shoes and scrapers before ordering, since those are the pieces gravel wears out first. It is the right choice when the budget is tight and the lane is short.
products.bestFor: Budget gravel drives with packed snow.
pros: Serrated steel augers bite into packed snow
Six forward and two reverse speeds

products.name: SENIX 40V 21-inch cordless blower, steel auger
products.description:
This is a single-stage machine, so it is not for the gravel itself. It makes sense only if your property mixes gravel and paved sections, such as a paved apron or walkway, and you want a light machine for the paved part.

A steel auger with variable speed is tougher than rubber, but on gravel it will still throw stones. Use it on pavement and leave the gravel to a two-stage or a shovel.

It is listed here to make the point clearly: single-stage machines and gravel do not mix. Keep it on the paved portion and use a shovel or a two-stage on the stone, which is the only way to avoid throwing gravel.
products.bestFor: Paved aprons and walks on a mixed gravel property.
cons: Not for the gravel surface itself

buyingCriteria.explanation: On gravel the auger housing must be able to sit above the surface, which a single-stage cannot do because its auger contacts the ground. The Husqvarna, EGO SNT2425, PowerSmart and BILT HARD are two-stage and let you set a gap. This is the single most important criterion for gravel. Many owners set the housing too low on the first storm and scalp a layer of stone off the drive. Start high, then lower it a quarter inch at a time until the machine clears cleanly. Treat the design choice as final, because no setting turns a single-stage into a gravel machine. It is better to buy a two-stage once than to replace a single-stage after a season of thrown stones.

Skid shoes set the height of the housing. On gravel, raise them about an inch so the machine leaves a thin layer of snow rather than scraping stone. Worn shoes drop the housing and scalp the drive, so inspect them each season. Check the shoes every few hours of use on gravel, because they wear far faster than on pavement. A pair of spares in the garage saves a trip to the dealer. Check how easy the shoes are to adjust and replace: a pair that needs a wrench and ten minutes is one you will actually set correctly, while a stubborn pair stays wrong all winter.

Tires or tracks decide whether the machine pulls or spins on gravel. The Husqvarna has 13-inch snow tires; the PowerSmart and BILT HARD list similar. For slopes, consider chains or tracks. Slopes and loose footing cause more wheel spin than flat pavement. Tire chains and a little weight on the handle help the machine pull instead of spin. Gravel drives often have soft edges and ruts, so a machine that can be steered by hand and holds a straight line on its own is worth the extra weight.

Steel and serrated augers, as on the PowerSmart and BILT HARD, cope with stone better than plastic. A taller intake such as the Husqvarna's 21 inches lets you take a tall pile without lowering the housing. Packed snow on a gravel drive is full of grit, which dulls plain augers quickly. Serrated or steel flights stay sharper for longer and are easier to replace. Dull augers leave a ridge down the middle of the pass, which is a good sign it is time to replace them.

Gravel lanes tend to be long. Gas gives unlimited runtime, while battery models like the EGO run for a limited time and draw more on loose footing. A long lane means a long run, so size your fuel or packs for the worst day. Gas wins on very long lanes because you refill in a minute. Remember that a gas machine can sit for a week between storms, while batteries need a charging routine; match the power to how often you clear.

Stones can come through the chute, so aim it away from windows, cars and people. A long throw like the PowerSmart's 45 feet puts snow far from the drive. Always check where the chute is aimed before you start. Even a two-stage can throw an occasional stone, and a car or window is easily damaged. Throw direction is as much about safety as snow: keep it away from cars, windows and neighbours.

howWeEvaluated.title: Design fit for gravel
howWeEvaluated.description: We kept only machines that can raise the housing, and placed the single-stage SENIX in a clearly limited role. That means the single-stage SENIX is kept only as a paved-section tool.

howWeEvaluated.title: Housing and shoes
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at intake height and adjustable skid shoes, since they decide how much stone ends up in the chute. Shoes are the part that decides whether a machine is suited to the surface. We also considered how easy the shoes are to reach and swap.

howWeEvaluated.title: Traction
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared tires and drive speeds, because loose footing makes traction the main limit. Loose footing means a tire that grips is worth more than a bigger motor.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership burden
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on the spec sheet and owner feedback patterns, we weighed gas upkeep, pack care and the extra wear that stone causes. Stone adds wear on every moving part, so upkeep matters more here.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit to drive
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched each model to a gravel lane length and snow depth. This is an editorial assessment, not a measured score. We recommend sizing for the longest lane you clear. A longer lane and a steeper grade would push us to the bigger engines in the list.

howToChoose.note: Even a two-stage needs the shoes set right.
howToChoose.intro: Gravel length is the first filter because it decides engine or pack size.

howToChoose.note: Measure the lane first. Match the shoe setting to the stone size.
howToChoose.intro: Gravel machines cost more than paved-drive machines, so compare within the two-stage class.

cards.label: Two-stage
cards.text: The Husqvarna, EGO SNT2425, PowerSmart and BILT HARD can raise the housing above the stone and throw snow with an impeller. They are the right tool for gravel.

cards.label: Single-stage
cards.text: The SENIX 21-inch uses an auger that touches the ground, so on gravel it throws stones. It is fine for paved sections only. Test on a small section. Gas is the easy choice for a lane over 150 feet.

howToChoose.note: Choose a two-stage for any gravel surface; keep single-stage machines on pavement.
Pick by the lane, not the brand. Test before the first storm.
howToChoose.intro: Fuel and packs each have limits on a long lane.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Snow tires, wheel drive and enough weight to bite. Chains or tracks help on a steep slope.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Husqvarna ST124 has 13-inch snow tires, and the PowerSmart 252cc adds engine headroom for a climb. A steep lane may need chains. Check chain fit before the first ice.

cards.text: Your gravel lane is long. The PowerSmart 26-inch or Husqvarna saves time every storm.

maintenance.why: Gravel wears shoes quickly. Replace them when they thin. Keep a spare pair in the garage.
Stone chips the bar and leaves a ridge. Look for chips and bends after each storm.
Fresh oil protects the engine in cold starts. Warm oil flows better in cold starts.
Stale fuel clogs the carburetor. A full tank with stabilizer stores best.
A stone can shear a pin, so carry spares. Spare pins cost little and save a storm. Wait for the auger to stop before you reach in.

faq.q: Can I use a single-stage on gravel?
faq.a: No. Its auger touches the surface and throws stones. Use a two-stage with raised skid shoes. The housing has to be able to lift off the surface, which only a two-stage allows. If you are unsure, a two-stage is the safest buy for any loose surface.

faq.q: How high should the skid shoes be?
faq.a: About an inch above the stone. That leaves a thin layer of snow instead of scraping the gravel. Measure with a coin: roughly the thickness of two coins is about right. A smaller gap leaves less snow but throws more stone.

An occasional stone can shear a pin or chip the scraper. Carry spares and inspect the shoes. Stones are the main cause of broken pins and chipped scrapers. A bent scraper bar is the first sign of trouble.
Gas has unlimited runtime. Battery is quieter but loose footing draws more current. Keep an eye on runtime on a long lane. Pack runtime shrinks quickly on loose footing and in packed snow.
Not for flat gravel. A steep or icy slope benefits from tracks or chains. Chains cost far less than tracks and work well on a modest grade. A set of chains also helps on ice.

faq.q: How do I avoid throwing stones?
faq.a: Raise the housing, clear slowly and aim the chute away from windows and cars. Clear slowly so the impeller throws snow rather than stone. A shovel is the right tool for the last inch on gravel.
